title: The 45-minute LLD answer
idea: A 45-minute low-level design (LLD) framework splits the interview into timed phases, so you finish with a running core and a design you can defend.

analogy.text: A cooking-show slot has fixed segments: prep on camera, cook the main dish, then plate and explain. Nobody spends forty minutes chopping onions.
analogy.breaks: The interviewer changes the recipe halfway; a show rarely does.

points: Spend the first five minutes on questions; agreed use cases become your demo script.
Model with enums, records and one interface per variation point before writing logic.
In a coding round, get one use case running by minute 30.
Follow-ups test extensibility: show a new rule is a new class, not an edit.

items.label: 0-5 min: Clarify
items.text: Ask about actors, must-have use cases and scope. Write the agreed list down.

items.label: 5-10 min: Entities
items.text: Nouns become classes. Fixed sets become enums; unchanging values become records.

items.label: 10-15 min: Contracts
items.text: Sketch the class diagram. Add an interface wherever behaviour will vary.

items.label: 15-30 min: Core
items.text: Code the main use case end to end, guards included. Skip boilerplate.

items.label: 30-40 min: Follow-ups
items.text: Handle twists: a new rule, bad input, two users. Name the class that changes.

items.label: 40-45 min: Wrap-up
items.text: Summarise trade-offs, the tests you would write, and what comes next.

code.title: Minute 30: the core
code.caption: A vending machine prompt at the end of the core phase: every agreed use case runs from `main`.

walk.text: `main` replays the use cases agreed in minute five. This is your live demo, not a test suite.
Enums fix the slots and statuses. `select` returns an `Outcome` value, so callers decide how to display it.
`Product` is an immutable record that rejects a missing name or a non-positive price at construction.
State lives in private `EnumMap` fields. Only `restock` and `select` change stock; nothing outside can.
`insert` accepts any value. Name this gap aloud and park it; it is a likely follow-up.
Guards first: sold out, then not enough credit with the exact shortfall. The interviewer sees edge cases handled.
The happy path is last and short: take one item, compute change, clear the credit.

code.title: Minute 35: follow-ups
code.caption: Two typical twists: a new pricing rule and a bad coin. The machine is trimmed to the parts the twists touch, and it takes a `PricingRule`, the interface you drew at minute 15.

walk.text: The happy-hour request becomes a second `PricingRule` passed in. The machine code does not change.
Draw this interface at minute 15, even if the core only uses list price.
`PercentOff` checks its range once. Integer cents avoid float error; division rounds down, so say so aloud.
The rule arrives by constructor injection and is checked for null. The field is final.
The parked gap is closed: `insert` rejects zero and negative coins with a message naming the value.
The demo tries a good coin and two bad ones. Credit counts only the accepted coin.

pitfalls: Coding before agreeing use cases; at minute 30 you find you built the wrong feature.
Drawing twelve classes and running none; the interviewer never sees anything work.
Typing in silence; narrate each decision so the interviewer can grade your reasoning.

quiz.q: Minute 22: entities exist but no use case runs yet. The interviewer asks about thread safety. Your best move?
options: Add synchronized to every method right away
Say it is out of scope for this interview
Answer briefly, note it, finish the core first
Rewrite the maps as ConcurrentHashMap before continuing
quiz.why: A short answer shows you know the issue; noting it keeps it on the follow-up list. A running core by minute 30 matters more than early hardening.

takeaway: Clarify, model, run one use case, then extend: watch the clock.

starters: What questions should I ask in the first five minutes?
What if I am still coding the core at minute 35?
How much of the class diagram should I draw before coding?
